yevamot-14a-11-13.note: Rabbi Abbahu would move an oil lamp on Shabbat when visiting the town of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who allowed it, but not in the town of Rabbi Yoḥanan, who forbade it. The Gemara explains that Abbahu himself agreed with the permissive view, but out of respect for Rabbi Yoḥanan he did not do it in his town. He also told his servant why, so the servant would not copy the lenient behavior there.

terms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion and analysis of the earlier Mishnah.

yevamot-15a-15-15.note: When the daughter-in-law of Shammai the Elder gave birth, Shammai removed part of the ceiling plaster and put branch covering over the bed, as if making a sukka (the booth used on the Sukkot festival) for the newborn. This was raised as proof that Shammai's school really acted on its own rulings. The Gemara answers that onlookers would simply think he wanted fresh air, so it proves nothing.

terms.meaning: A temporary booth with a leafy roof, in which people eat and sit during the festival of Sukkot.
The school of Shammai, which often disagreed with the school of Hillel.

yevamot-15a-16-16.note: The Yehu water trough in Jerusalem was linked by a hole to a ritual bath, and people used it for purifying utensils. Beit Shammai sent messengers who widened the hole, since in their view it only counts as connected if most of the barrier is open. This is offered as evidence that Beit Shammai acted on their own rulings. The passage ends with the widening, and states no answer to the objection.

terms.meaning: A pool of water used for ritual purification.
The school of Shammai, which often disagreed with the school of Hillel.

yevamot-15b-1-4.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok saw his teacher, Rabbi Yoḥanan the Ḥorani, eating only dry bread and salt in a drought year. He brought olives, but the teacher politely refused them, fearing they were damp and so ritually impure. Elazar's father explained that the olive barrel had a hole that later got clogged, so the olives were not made susceptible to impurity. The passage ends by noting the teacher always followed Beit Hillel, and concludes that Beit Shammai did generally act on their own rulings.

terms.meaning: A status that makes food or objects unfit for certain holy uses until purified; liquids on food can make it susceptible.
A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

yevamot-16a-2-11.note: The Sages heard that the elderly, blind Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas had ruled that a certain woman was permitted. A group (Rabbis Yehoshua, Elazar ben Azarya and Akiva) visited him, and he said the law follows Beit Hillel; the other ruling, he explained, came from his sharp younger brother Yonatan. Leaving by three doors, they looked for Yonatan, and Akiva met him and answered all his objections. Yonatan then insulted Akiva, who replied modestly that he had not reached even the level of shepherds.

people.name: Yonatan ben Harkinas
people.about: Dosa's younger brother and a disciple of Shammai

terms.meaning: A law case about whether the co-wife of a man's daughter is permitted to his brothers for levirate marriage, which Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disputed.
The school of Hillel, which often disagreed with the school of Shammai.

yevamot-21b-1-2.note: Rav Ḥisda recalls hearing Rabbi Ami say, when he was young, that a daughter-in-law was forbidden only because of another daughter-in-law, and he did not understand it. Astrologers told him he would be a teacher, so he reasoned that either he would understand it himself or could ask others. Now he understands it as follows: the ban on one's daughter's daughter-in-law was made so she would not be confused with one's son's daughter-in-law, and it does not extend further.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: the teacher he heard it from

terms.meaning: Star-readers who claimed to predict a person's future.

yevamot-25b-4-4.note: An armed bandit being led out for execution told bystanders to tell the wife of Shimon the Priest that he had killed her husband near Lod, and the court allowed her to remarry on that basis. This was brought as proof that a murderer's own statement is accepted. Rabbi Yehuda rejected the proof: the bandit had said only that he was with the murderers, not that he did the killing himself.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

yevamot-31a-11-11.note: A man called Bar Shatya, who sometimes went insane, sold property. Two witnesses said he was sane at the time, and two said he was insane, so the sale was either valid or void. Rav Ashi ruled that the two pairs cancel each other out and the land stays with Bar Shatya. The Gemara uses this to say that when there is no proof about a betrothal or divorce, the woman keeps her earlier status.

people.name: Bar Shatya
people.about: a man who would occasionally go insane

terms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion and analysis of the earlier Mishnah.

yevamot-32b-5-10.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya and Bar Kappara disagreed about whether someone who breaks two prohibitions at once, such as a non-priest serving in the Temple on Shabbat, is punished once or twice. Each jumped up and swore by the Temple service that he had heard his view from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and this repeated over three cases. Rabbi Ḥiyya then reasoned it out, and the Gemara tries several explanations of what they argued about. It ends with an unresolved difficulty and says plainly that it is difficult.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: the teacher both claim to quote

terms.meaning: Guilty of breaking two separate prohibitions with one act, and so punished for both.
Someone who is not from the priestly family, and so may not do the Temple service.

yevamot-34b-7-7.note: A woman came to Rav Yosef and said she had waited ten years after her husband's death and still gave birth. Rav Yosef told her not to cast doubt on the Sages' statement, which holds that a pregnancy cannot last that long. She then confessed that she had had intercourse with a non-Jew during those ten years.

yevamot-37b-5-8.note: Rav, visiting Dardeshir, and Rav Naḥman, visiting Shakhnetziv, each announced that he wanted a woman to be his wife for the day, apparently showing that this was allowed. The Gemara replies that famous Sages are different, since their children are always known as the Sage's. It then explains that they sent word seven days ahead so the women could count seven clean days before marrying, or that they only meant to be in private with the woman and avoid improper thoughts.

people.name: Rava
people.about: cited for the rule about seven clean days

terms.meaning: A woman who may have had a menstrual flow counts seven days without any flow and then immerses in a ritual bath before she may be with her husband.

yevamot-41b-7-8.note: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether a widow could perform ḥalitza (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) within three months of her husband's death, even if she might be pregnant. Rabbi Yosei said no. He cited the verse 'And if the man does not wish to take his yevama', meaning ḥalitza is only possible for a woman with whom levirate marriage would also be possible, and that includes a woman temporarily barred from marrying, such as in the first three months.

terms.meaning: A ceremony in which a brother-in-law is released from the duty to marry his brother's childless widow.
A childless widow who is bound to her late husband's brother.

yevamot-45a-3-3.note: Rabbi Aḥa and Rabbi Tanḥum ransomed captives from Armon and brought them to Tiberias. One woman had become pregnant by a non-Jew, and they asked Rabbi Ami what the child's status would be. He answered that Rabbi Yoḥanan, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Ḥanina all say that the child of a non-Jew or slave and a Jewish woman is a mamzer.

terms.meaning: A person born from certain forbidden unions, who is not allowed to marry into the wider Jewish community (a few narrow exceptions apply).

yevamot-45a-11-15.note: A man asked Rav about the status of a child of a non-Jew or slave and a Jewish woman, and Rav said the child's lineage is unflawed. The man, who was such a child, asked to marry Rav's daughter, but Rav refused, and Rav's grandson pointed out that this seemed to contradict his own ruling. Rav said he refused for other reasons, but the man kept pleading and would not leave. In the end Rav fixed his eyes on him and the man died.

terms.meaning: A small measure of grain or produce.

yevamot-45b-6-6.note: Ravina reports that Rabbi Yosei bar Avin, visiting a town, ruled that the child of an unmarried woman and a slave was fit to marry into the community, but the child of a married woman and a slave was a mamzeret. Rav Sheshet quotes it differently: the Sage was Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Zevida, and he ruled both children fit. Another Sage then says Ameimar likewise ruled both fit. The passage ends with these competing reports and no decision.

terms.meaning: The female form of mamzer: a person born from certain forbidden unions, who may not marry into the wider Jewish community.

yevamot-45b-8-8.note: Rava ruled that Rav Mari bar Raḥel, whose father was not Jewish and whose mother was, was fit to marry into the community. He also appointed him as an official in Babylonia. The Gemara notes that officials must come from among 'your brethren', but since his mother was Jewish, he counts as such and was eligible.

people.name: Rava
people.about: made the ruling and the appointment

people.name: Rav Mari bar Raḥel
people.about: son of a non-Jewish father and a Jewish mother

terms.meaning: Officials or administrators appointed for the Jewish community.

yevamot-46a-2-2.note: A convert named Beloreya had slaves who immersed in the ritual bath for conversion before she did. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that the slaves had acquired themselves and become free. Rav Ḥisda used this to raise a difficulty: it seems that had they immersed after her, they would not have become free. This conflicts with an earlier explanation in the Gemara.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.
Dipping in a ritual bath, a required step in conversion and in freeing a slave owned by a non-Jew.

yevamot-46a-9-9.note: Rav Ashi wished to have his slave Minyamin immersed in the ritual bath and gave him to Ravina and Rav Aḥa. He warned that he would claim compensation from them if they did not stop the slave from immersing for conversion. They put a bridle on the slave's neck, loosened it at the moment of immersion, then tightened it again right away while he was still in the water.

terms.meaning: A bridle or restraint placed on the neck.

yevamot-46a-13-14.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba visited Gavla and saw several things that troubled the rules: women pregnant by men who were circumcised but had not yet immersed to finish converting, wine being poured by non-Jews, and lupines cooked by non-Jews that Jews were eating. He said nothing there, but reported it to Rabbi Yoḥanan. Rabbi Yoḥanan told him to announce publicly that the children were mamzerim and the wine and lupines forbidden, being strict because the townspeople were not learned and might otherwise slip into real violations.

terms.meaning: A person born from certain forbidden unions, who is not allowed to marry into the wider Jewish community (a few narrow exceptions apply).
Dipping in a ritual bath, a required step in conversion.

yevamot-46b-13-13.note: In the house of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rabbi, a convert came who had been circumcised but had not yet immersed in the ritual bath. The Sage told him to stay until the next day, and then they would immerse him. The passage ends there, and it does not say the immersion happened or explain the reason for waiting, though it is used to show that the immersion is done before a court of several Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: another Sage present, according to one version

terms.meaning: Dipping in a ritual bath, a required step in conversion.

yevamot-47a-7-7.note: A man known as Jewish told Rabbi Yehuda that he had actually converted in private, so he was not truly Jewish. Rabbi Yehuda asked if he had witnesses, and he did not, and he had children. Rabbi Yehuda ruled that he is believed about himself, so he is barred from marrying a Jewish woman, but he is not believed in a way that would make his children unfit.

yevamot-59b-6-6.note: Rav Dimi reported from Eretz Yisrael that a girl in the village of Hitlu was sweeping her house when a hunting dog attacked her from behind. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled she was still permitted to marry a priest, because she was not considered a zona (a woman disqualified from marrying a priest). Shmuel added that she was even fit for a High Priest, since she was still considered a virgin, and the Gemara clarifies he meant she would be fit for one.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: brought the report from Eretz Yisrael

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: added that she is even fit for a High Priest

terms.meaning: A woman who has had a forbidden relationship and is therefore not allowed to marry a priest.

yevamot-60b-14-14.note: In a city in Eretz Yisrael, the lineage of one family was disputed, so Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent Rabbi Romanus to check. He found that the family included the daughter of a convert who had converted before the age of three years and a day, and who had married a priest. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allowed her to stay married to the priesthood, which shows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled like Rabbi Shimon, as Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi confirmed.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: sent Rabbi Romanus and permitted the woman

terms.term: less than three years and one day
terms.meaning: The age limit in this discussion: a girl who converts younger than this is treated as a virgin for the purpose of marrying a priest.

yevamot-60b-18-18.note: A priest married a woman who had converted before the age of three years and a day. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak asked him why he was breaking the law, and the priest answered that Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi quoted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi as ruling like Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, who allows it. Rav Naḥman told him to divorce her, or he would remove Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi from his ear, meaning he would act so the priest could no longer rely on that opinion.

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron, who is subject to stricter marriage rules.

yevamot-61a-7-7.note: The Mishnah mentioned Yehoshua ben Gamla, and the Gemara points out it says the king appointed him but not that he deserved it. Rav Yosef sees a scheme here: Rav Asi said that Marta bat Baitos brought King Yannai a vessel of gold coins (dinars), about half a se'a in size, until he made Yehoshua ben Gamla High Priest. So the appointment was political, bought with money, not made properly by the priests and the Sanhedrin.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: the king who made the appointment

terms.meaning: The chief priest who served in the Temple in Jerusalem.
The supreme court of the Jewish people.

yevamot-62b-3-4.note: The Gemara first says that having two grandchildren from one child does not fulfil the duty to have children. It then objects: the Rabbis once told Rav Sheshet to marry and have sons, and he answered that his daughter's sons count as his sons. The Gemara replies he was only brushing them off; the real reason was that he had become impotent from waiting so long through Rav Huna's very long lectures.

terms.meaning: The commandment to have children, which the rabbis discuss how to fulfil (for example, with a son and a daughter).

yevamot-62b-9-10.note: After Rabbi Akiva's students died, the world was empty of Torah until he went to the South and taught five new students: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua. They kept Torah study alive for later generations. The Gemara adds that the earlier students all died between Passover and Shavuot, of a 'bad death,' which Rav Nachman says was diphtheria.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: great teacher whose earlier students died

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: one of the five new students

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: one of the five new students

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: one of the five new students

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: one of the five new students

terms.meaning: The holiday about seven weeks after Passover.

yevamot-63a-11-12.note: Rabbi Chiyya wished Rav to be saved from something worse than death, and Rav found the verse about a woman more bitter than death. Rav's wife did the opposite of whatever he asked, such as cooking peas when he wanted lentils. When their son Chiyya grew up, he reversed Rav's requests when passing them on, so Rav got what he wanted. Rav praised the idea but told his son not to do it, since it means saying something untrue.

people.name: Rav
people.about: returned from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.

yevamot-63a-13-13.note: Rabbi Chiyya's wife constantly aggravated him, yet he brought her gifts. He told Rav it is enough that wives raise the children and keep their husbands from sin, so they deserve thanks. Then Rav Yehuda, teaching his son Rav Yitzchak the verse about a woman more bitter than death, said it described the son's own mother. The Gemara notes he also said a man finds peace only with his first wife, and resolves it: she was sharp but easily calmed.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it.

yevamot-64b-10-10.note: Rabbi Yochanan reported that in Tzippori, three sisters each circumcised a son and each baby died. The fourth sister asked Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who told her not to circumcise her son. The Gemara learns from this that he held a pattern becomes an established presumption only after it happens three times.

terms.meaning: A legal assumption that something will happen again, based on past repetition.

yevamot-64b-13-13.note: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reported an incident before Rabbi Yochanan in the synagogue of Maon, on a Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbat. Two sisters had each circumcised a son who then died. When the third sister came, Rabbi Yochanan told her to go ahead and circumcise her son, because a presumption of danger is not established after only two cases. This settles the question of whether two occurrences are enough.

people.name: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
people.about: came from Eretz Yisrael and reported the incident

terms.meaning: A legal assumption that something will happen again, based on past repetition.
The Land of Israel.

yevamot-64b-15-15.note: Relying on the ruling that a presumption needs three cases, Abaye married Chuma, whose first two husbands had both died. He did not worry that she was a woman whose husbands die. Abaye died while married to her as well.

people.name: Chuma
people.about: daughter of Isi; her first two husbands had died

people.name: Rav Yitzchak, son of Rabba bar bar Chana

yevamot-65b-14-14.note: A woman came to Rabbi Ami asking for a divorce and her marriage-contract payment because her husband could not father children. He first said she was not commanded to have children, so she had no claim. She replied that without children no one would care for her in old age, and he then said that in such a case the husband is forced to divorce her and pay.

terms.meaning: The document and payment a husband owes his wife, due upon divorce.
The commandment to have children, which the Gemara says applies to men, not women.

yevamot-65b-15-15.note: A woman asked Rav Nachman for a divorce because her husband could not father children. He said she was not commanded to have children. She answered that she needs a staff for her hand and a hoe for her burial, meaning children to support her in old age and bury her. Rav Nachman agreed that in such a case the husband is forced to divorce her.

terms.meaning: The commandment to have children, which the Gemara says applies to men, not women.

yevamot-65b-15-17.note: The first part repeats the woman before Rav Nachman, who forces the husband to divorce her. The second part tells of Rabbi Chiyya's wife Yehudit, who suffered greatly giving birth to twin sons born two months apart. She disguised herself, asked Rabbi Chiyya if a woman must have children, heard no, and drank a potion to become infertile. When he found out, he wished she had borne one more set of twins, since their sons and daughters all became leading scholars or mothers of scholars.

yevamot-66a-1-1.note: A woman who was half-slave and half-free could marry neither a slave nor a Jew. Her master was forced to free her completely. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak gave a different reason: because she could not marry, she was behaving immorally, and the court acted to save her and others from sin. The Gemara uses this to ask whether the reason was to let her have children.

terms.meaning: A non-Jewish slave owned by a Jew, who had a different legal status from a Jew.
To free a slave.

yevamot-66b-7-8.note: A woman brought a fine wool robe into her marriage, listed in her marriage contract. After her husband died, his orphaned children used the robe to cover his body as a shroud, and she demanded it back. Rava ruled that the dead man had acquired it, and it is forbidden to benefit from something set aside for the dead. When challenged with another ruling, Rav Kahana answered that the robe had not yet been collected by the woman, so it still belonged to the husband's estate and his heirs could make it a shroud.

people.name: Rava
people.about: ruled the robe was acquired by the dead man

people.name: Nanai, son of Rav Yosef, son of Rava

terms.meaning: Property a wife brings into marriage that the husband takes responsibility for, and must pay back its value.
A cloth wrapped around or spread over a dead body for burial.

yevamot-72b-3-6.note: Rabbi Yochanan taught that notar, leftover sacrificial meat that must be burned, is burned only by day when burned at its proper time. Rabbi Elazar objected with a baraita about circumcision, which reads the word 'and' in a verse as extending the rule to other cases, and said the same hint appears for notar. Rabbi Yochanan had no answer. Afterward he told Reish Lakish how impressive this was, and Reish Lakish said it is a baraita found in Torat Kohanim. Rabbi Yochanan then learned the whole book in three days.

terms.meaning: Meat of an offering left over past its allowed time, which must be burned.
A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it.
An ancient commentary on the Book of Leviticus.

yevamot-75a-18-18.note: The Gemara asks whether a man whose testicles were merely punctured is unable to have children, and recalls a man whose testicles were pierced by a palm-tree thorn while he climbed. The man later had children. The Gemara answers that Shmuel sent this case to Rav, who told him to investigate where the children came from, doubting the man could father children and suspecting his wife had committed adultery.

people.name: Rav
people.about: told him to inquire about the children

terms.meaning: A physical injury that makes a man legally barred from marrying into the congregation of Israel.

yevamot-75b-15-15.note: In Mata Mechasya, a man's member was cut open like a gutter. Mar bar Rav Ashi trimmed the flesh into the shape of a quill and so ruled him fit to marry into the congregation. A second case in Pumbedita involved a man with a blocked seminal duct who emitted semen through the urinary duct. Rav Beivai bar Abaye was inclined to rule him fit because he was not crushed or severed, and Rav Pappi began to respond, but the text breaks off.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: inclined to rule the second man fit

terms.meaning: To be permitted to marry a Jewish woman of full status; some injuries bar a man from this.

yevamot-77a-0-0.note: Doeg raised objections about other people barred from the congregation, and the sages could not answer. He then wanted to announce that David was barred, since David descended from Ruth the Moabite. He was answered at once: the tradition is that the ban applies to Ammonite and Moabite men, not women. The text connects this to Amasa, whose father is called both an Israelite and an Ishmaelite, which Rava explains by saying he girded his sword like an Arab and threatened anyone who rejected the ruling.

people.name: David
people.about: the one Doeg wanted to disqualify

people.name: Amasa
people.about: his father is named in two verses

terms.meaning: To be permitted to marry a Jew of full status.

yevamot-77b-8-9.note: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came from Eretz Yisrael and reported a baraita taught before Rabbi Yochanan about whether Ammonite women and their children are fit to marry into the congregation. Rabbi Yochanan told him to go teach it outside the study hall, meaning it is not accepted law. He said the first part was already well known and the second was unnecessary, since the son of an Ammonite is simply an Ammonite.

people.name: Rabbi Zakkai
people.about: taught the baraita before Rabbi Yochanan

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it.
A member of the ancient nation of Ammon; Ammonite men may not marry into the congregation, but the women may.

yevamot-78a-12-12.note: Rava cited a baraita in which Rabbi Yehuda recalls his friend Minyamin, an Egyptian convert who studied with Rabbi Akiva. Minyamin said he married another first-generation Egyptian convert and planned to marry his son to a second-generation one so that his grandson would be fit to marry into the congregation. This seemed to challenge a rule, but the Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan told the teacher of the baraita to say instead that Minyamin sought to marry his son to a first-generation convert.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: an Egyptian convert and student of Rabbi Akiva

people.name: Rabbi Yochanan
people.about: corrected the wording of the baraita

terms.meaning: To be permitted to marry a Jew of full status.
A rabbi of the Mishnah period; here, one who recites such teachings by heart.

yevamot-78b-11-11.note: Rabbi Ami investigated a man in his neighborhood and declared him a mamzer, a person born from a forbidden union who is barred from marrying most Jews. The man went around weeping. Rabbi Ami told him not to be upset, because by making it publicly known he had given him life. The text says that once someone is publicly known as a mamzer, he and his descendants may survive.

terms.meaning: A person born from certain forbidden unions, who is barred from marrying most Jews.

yevamot-86b-2-2.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, a priest, took the first tithe from a certain garden, since he held that priests are also entitled to it. Rabbi Akiva closed the garden and moved its entrance to face a cemetery, which a priest may not enter, to keep him out. Rabbi Elazar joked about Akiva, the former shepherd, and asked where his own livelihood would come from. The text adds that he was in fact very rich and was making a point about being blocked from what he saw as his due.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: closed the garden and moved the entrance

terms.meaning: A tenth of the harvest given to the Levites; Rabbi Elazar held priests may take it too.
Priests are forbidden to enter burial places because of ritual impurity.

yevamot-90b-9-9.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov taught that the court may sometimes punish where the Torah does not require it, to build a fence around the Torah. As an example, in the time of the Greeks a man rode a horse on Shabbat, which was forbidden only by rabbinic law. The court stoned him as a Shabbat violator, not because he deserved it, but because Jews at that time were careless about Shabbat and the hour demanded it.

terms.meaning: A rabbinic rule or measure meant to keep people far from breaking a Torah law.

yevamot-90b-10-10.note: A man had relations with his own wife under a fig tree in plain sight. The court brought him in and flogged him, though the Torah does not forbid relations with one's wife, because the hour required it, to discourage others from licentious behavior. The Gemara raises that this shows a court can set aside a Torah law, and answers that safeguarding the law is a special case, as with the prophet Elijah.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: the prophet, given as a precedent

terms.meaning: A court punishment of lashes.

yevamot-93a-7-8.note: Rabbi Yannai's sharecropper brought him a basket of fruit every Shabbat eve. One day he was late, so Rabbi Yannai separated tithes in advance for the fruit he expected, so as not to be unable to tithe on Shabbat. Unsure that this works for fruit not yet in hand, he asked Rabbi Chiyya, who said he had acted well and gave a source. Rabbi Yannai worried because a dream had shown him the words 'bruised reed.' Rabbi Chiyya said the dream referred to a verse about the Messiah, meaning he had acted rightly.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce that must be set aside for priests, Levites, or the poor before the food may be eaten.
A farmer who works the owner's land and pays him part of the harvest.

yevamot-96b-13-17.note: Rabbi Elazar taught a law in the study hall without saying it came from his teacher, Rabbi Yohanan, who got angry. Two colleagues tried to calm him with a story about two sages who tore a Torah scroll in anger, which only made him angrier. Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi then compared it to Joshua, who taught Moses' Torah without always naming Moses, and Yohanan was appeased. The text explains Yohanan cared because a teaching quoted in a scholar's name keeps his lips moving in the grave.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Yohanan's student, who taught without naming him

people.name: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
people.about: two colleagues who tried and failed to calm him

terms.meaning: a point of Jewish law
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-98a-3-3.note: The Gemara quotes a teaching about Niftayim, a convert who married the wife of his maternal half brother, and the Sages said such a marriage is not valid for a convert. The Gemara objects that this cannot mean no convert's marriage ever counts, so it rewords the teaching: a convert is not bound by the usual ban on a brother's wife. It then suggests this applies where the brother was also a convert when he married her.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: the sage who reports the incident

terms.meaning: the discussion in the Talmud that analyzes the Mishnah

yevamot-98a-5-5.note: Ben Yasiyan reports that overseas he met a convert married to his maternal half brother's widow and asked who permitted it. The convert answered that Rabbi Akiva, sitting on a bench in that place, had allowed it for a local woman and her seven sons. The Gemara uses this as another proof that a convert may marry his maternal brother's wife, perhaps where the brother was also a convert.

people.name: Ben Yasiyan
people.about: the traveler who tells the story

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: the sage said to have permitted the marriage

terms.meaning: a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-99b-9-10.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok says he testified in court only once, and on his word a slave was given the presumed status of a priest. That sounds like a mistake, but the Gemara asks whether the court could really have done that. It reasons that if God does not let even the animals of righteous people cause harm, He would not let the righteous themselves cause an error.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: the sage who gave the testimony

terms.meaning: a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-101b-3-3.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalls sitting before Rabbi Tarfon when a widow came to perform halitza, the ceremony that releases her from marrying her late husband's brother. Rabbi Tarfon told the students to call out 'He who had his shoe removed' once it was done. The Gemara uses this to explain a verse saying all who witness the ceremony must respond that way.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: the sage who gave the instruction

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a widow whose husband died childless and who is tied to his brother

yevamot-101b-14-14.note: Rav Ashi came to Rav Kahana's house, and Rav Kahana asked him to join a group of five to perform halitza. Rav Kahana added that his own teacher Rav Yehuda had once told him to go to the bundle of reeds, the set place for such cases. When asked why five were needed when three would do, Rav Yehuda said it was to make the matter public, not because the law requires it.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Kahana's teacher in the account

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry

yevamot-101b-15-16.note: Rav Yehuda asked Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to join the five men watching a halitza ceremony. Shmuel pointed out that the law requires a court of Jews who are Jews from birth, and he admitted he was a convert along with his father. Rav Yehuda praised his honesty, saying he would accept his word to cancel a debt document, and the Gemara clarifies that one man's word cannot collect money.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: said he was a convert, so he could not serve

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry

yevamot-102a-7-8.note: Rabbi Yosei tells of visiting Netzivin in Babylonia and meeting an Elder who knew Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, a local sage. The Elder had seen him perform halitza many times and said a soft leather shoe is not allowed, since the Torah says 'his shoe' and not 'from his shoe'. Rabbi Yosei then asked why Rabbi Meir ruled such a halitza valid, and the account ends on that question.

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-102b-13-14.note: A heretic told Rabban Gamliel that God had given up on the Jewish people the way a brother-in-law performs halitza, citing a verse from Hosea that says God 'removed Himself from them'. Rabban Gamliel called him a fool and pointed out the verse says 'from them', so it is Israel that removed itself from God. He added that in halitza the shoe removal by the brother-in-law means nothing to the widow's status, so this abandonment has no weight.

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a person who rejects the rabbis' teachings

yevamot-103b-5-6.note: Abaye stood before Rav Yosef when a widow came for halitza, and Rav Yosef asked Abaye for his sandal for the ceremony. Abaye gave his left one, and Rav Yosef noted that a left shoe is only acceptable after the fact. Abaye replied that the same is true of a borrowed shoe, and Rav Yosef said that was his point: give the shoe as a temporary gift so it is truly his, making the ceremony ideal.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: asked for it and set the rule

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
from the start, as the ideal way, as opposed to 'after the fact' when it is only acceptable

yevamot-105a-5-7.note: A woman spat before taking off the brother-in-law's shoe, which is the wrong order for halitza, and Rabbi Ami said she need not spit again. Rabbi Abba bar Memel objected, but Rabbi Ami warned that repeating it could lead people to wrongly permit a woman who has already done halitza. Rabbi Abba thought he was dodging, but afterwards he checked and found a teaching that the ceremony counts either way.

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-105a-8-9.note: Levi went to villages to teach and was asked three questions he could not answer, so he returned to the study hall. They told him that the Torah does not say the shoe must be removed by hand, so an armless woman may do halitza. They also said it says only 'she shall spit', not saliva, so spitting blood is valid. The text gives no answer to the third question, about writing in Heaven that is not truth.

people.name: Levi
people.about: went to teach in the villages

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry

yevamot-105a-14-14.note: A Jerusalem family kept losing its children around age eighteen and went to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai. He said they might descend from the house of Eli, whose descendants were told they would die as young men, and advised them to immerse themselves in Torah study. They did, lived longer lives, and were called the family of Yohanan.

people.name: Eli
people.about: a biblical priest whose house was told its men would die young

terms.meaning: a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-105b-3-10.note: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi entered the study hall, the heavy Rabbi Yishmael stepped over seated students to reach his place, and the attendant Abdon mocked him. Yishmael answered sharply, then offered a ruling that spared Abdon a trip to check a young woman's age, and rebuked him for stepping over heads without need. Abdon was told to stand still, and the text says he was then struck with leprosy and his two newly married sons drowned. Rav Nahman says this suffering cleansed his sins.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
Abdon
people.about: short for Abba Yudan, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's student and attendant

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: head of the study hall, called Rabbi

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Yishmael's father, whose rulings he quotes

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a widow whose husband died childless and who is tied to his brother

yevamot-106a-3-3.note: A widow had to deal with her brother-in-law, who was not suitable for her. The judges had her perform halitza on the condition that she pay him two hundred dinars. She never paid, and the case came to Rabbi Hiyya, who ruled the halitza valid anyway.

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a brother-in-law of a childless widow, who may marry her or release her

yevamot-106a-4-5.note: A man brought his brother's widow to Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba so the court could press her to marry him. She told Rabbi Hiyya she knew the man was after her money and would not be good for her. Rabbi Hiyya told the man that she would remove his shoe as a form of marriage, which was really halitza, and it left her forbidden to him forever. He then asked the man to allow a second, proper halitza so she could marry others.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: the sage who handled the case

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: his view is that a halitza done under a mistaken belief does not count

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
the brother-in-law and the childless widow tied to him

yevamot-106a-6-10.note: Rav Pappa's sister-in-law was tied to a brother-in-law who was not suitable, and Abaye had him do halitza on the condition that she pay two hundred dinars. After it was done, Rav Pappa argued she had only been fooling him, and cited a teaching about a prisoner promising a ferryman too much, so she owed nothing. Abaye agreed. Amazed at the young man's sharpness, Abaye asked about his parents and, envious that his own were not alive, looked on them, and both died.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: the judge who heard the case

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: a young man who argued on his sister-in-law's behalf

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-106b-7-8.note: Rav Ashi found Rav Kahana carefully coaching a widow to say the halitza words 'he did not wish to consummate the levirate marriage' in one piece. Rav Ashi asked whether he did not follow Rava, who said proper pausing is not essential. Rav Kahana replied that Rava agrees this line must be said properly, and quoted Abaye's wording for the written halitza record.

people.name: Rava and Abaye
people.about: earlier sages whose views are quoted

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
a widow whose husband died childless and who is tied to his brother

yevamot-108b-10-11.note: During Roman persecution, people wanted a ruling on whether a girl married as a minor, who left one husband by divorce and a second by refusal, could return to the first. They paid one messenger four hundred dinars to take the risky trip. Rabbi Akiva in prison and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin both said it is forbidden. The Gemara uses this to say which sage held that view.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: imprisoned by the Romans for teaching Torah

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: a sage in Netzivin, in Babylonia

terms.meaning: a declaration by a girl married as a minor that ends the marriage without a divorce document
a sage of the Mishnah era

yevamot-108b-14-14.note: A second version of the previous account says two messengers were hired for four hundred dinars. They asked Rabbi Akiva in prison and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin, and both ruled the case forbidden.

yevamot-110a-4-6.note: In Neresh a girl married as a minor grew up and was seated under the wedding canopy, but another man snatched her and married her. Rav's students did not require the second man to give her a divorce document. Rav Pappa says the first husband had already consummated the marriage; Rav Ashi says the snatcher acted wrongly, so the Sages cancelled his betrothal, even if done by intercourse, which they treated as a licentious act.

people.name: Rav Bruna and Rav Hananel
people.about: students of Rav who were there

people.name: Ravina
people.about: asked Rav Ashi a follow-up question

terms.meaning: the first stage of marriage, which makes the woman legally bound to the man
the document that ends a marriage

yevamot-112a-5-5.note: A brother-in-law and his brother's widow both said they had not consummated their levirate marriage and came before Rava. Rava told the Sages to arrange halitza for her. Rav Sherevya pointed out a teaching that she needs both a divorce document and halitza, and Rava said that if that teaching exists he takes back his ruling.

terms.meaning: a ceremony in which a widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe, freeing her to remarry
the brother-in-law and the childless widow tied to him
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that is not in the Mishnah itself

yevamot-113a-9-9.note: A deaf-mute man lived near Rav Malkiyyu, who arranged his marriage to a woman and wrote her a marriage contract of four hundred dinars from the man's property, though the man was not obligated to. Rava praised him as very wise. Rav Malkiyyu reasoned that if they would acquire a servant for the man, all the more so a wife who is both a servant and a spouse.

terms.meaning: the marriage contract that sets what a wife is owed if the marriage ends

yevamot-113b-15-15.note: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna lost the keys to the study hall, so on Shabbat they could not get in or bring a key through the public domain. Rabbi Pedat told him to lead boys and girls to where the keys were lost, so that if they found them they would bring them without being told. The Gemara says this fits a view that a court need not stop a child from breaking a prohibition. The text does not say if the keys were found.

terms.meaning: in Shabbat law, an open area where carrying objects is forbidden

yevamot-115a-3-3.note: At the end of a wedding, a fire breaks out in the bridal chamber. The bride screams for people to look at her husband, and they find a burnt, unrecognizable man lying there, with a palm of a hand nearby. The passage stops here, so the ruling on whether she may remarry is not in this text.

yevamot-115a-10-10.note: Two Torah scholars traveling with Abba Yosei ben Simai were on a boat that sank. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi let their wives remarry on the word of women who said the men had died. The Gemara objects: the sea is like a battlefield, where mistakes are possible, and women's testimony about a husband's death is normally weak, so it asks how he could rely on it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: a leading sage who permitted the wives to remarry

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

yevamot-115b-7-7.note: Yitzhak the Exilarch, a nephew of Rav Beivai, died while traveling from Cortva to Spain, and a message was sent from Spain reporting his death. The Gemara asks whether the report can be trusted given that another man might share the name Yitzhak. Abaye says we are concerned about this; Rava says we are not.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

yevamot-116b-3-3.note: A woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court, and the people there told her to mourn her husband, tear her clothes and unbind her hair so the court would believe her. The Gemara asks whether they were telling her to lie. It answers that they thought the law lets her remarry anyway, but feared Rabbi Yehuda would refuse unless she showed grief, so this would avoid trouble.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: the judge whose court she came to

yevamot-116b-9-9.note: At the end of the wheat harvest, ten people went out to harvest and a snake bit one, who died. His wife told the court he had died, and messengers found it was as she said. The sages then ruled that a woman who says her husband died may remarry on that basis. If he left no children and has a brother, she enters levirate marriage. This is the case Beit Hillel referred to.

terms.meaning: The duty of a childless man's brother to marry his widow.
The school of Hillel, whose opinions are often compared with Beit Shammai.

yevamot-116b-15-15.note: A person was carrying water and ashes of purification, made from the red heifer, across the Jordan River by boat. An olive-sized piece of a corpse was found stuck to the bottom of the boat, making the water and ashes ritually impure. In response the sages said that such things may not be carried on the Jordan River in a boat. The passage ends with a dispute over whether this applies to other similar cases or only this one.

terms.meaning: Ashes used with water to purify people who had contact with a corpse.
In a state that disqualifies something from holy use until purified.

yevamot-120a-10-10.note: Abba bar Marta owed money to members of the Exilarch's household, who were known to be violent, and did not want to be seen by them. He stuck wax onto a strip of worn cloth and attached it to his forehead to change his look. He walked past them and they did not recognize him. The Gemara draws the lesson that changing the forehead changes a person's face a great deal.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

yevamot-120b-7-7.note: The Gemara cites an incident in Asya where a man was lowered into the sea on a rope and only his leg came up. The Sages ruled that if the leg was cut off at or above the knee, his wife may remarry, since he could not survive that; if below the knee, she may not. The Gemara uses this to challenge whether the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

terms.meaning: The earlier collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses.

yevamot-121a-10-13.note: A man drowned in the lake at Samkei, and Rav Sheila let his wife remarry because witnesses saw him go in and not come out. Rav wanted to excommunicate Rav Sheila, but Shmuel suggested asking him first. Rav Sheila admitted he had erred: he thought the still water counted as having a visible edge, but waves could have carried the man out of sight. Shmuel and Rav then quoted verses praising each other's caution and advice.

people.name: Rav Sheila
people.about: the one who allowed the wife to remarry

terms.meaning: To formally ban someone from the community as punishment.
Water whose far edge cannot be seen; a man lost in it was not accepted as dead.

yevamot-121a-14-14.note: Two men were fishing with nets on the Jordan River, and one went into a cave with a fish pond. Night fell and he could not find the opening, so his friend thought he had drowned and told his family. The next morning the man found the exit and came home to find people mourning him. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said this shows how great the Sages' words are: a wife may remarry if her husband fell into water with a visible end, but not if it had no end.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: the sage who tells the incident

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

yevamot-121a-17-18.note: Rabban Gamliel saw a boat sink and grieved for the Torah scholar aboard, Rabbi Akiva. Later Akiva turned up on dry land teaching, and said a plank from the boat reached him and he bowed his head before each wave so none swept him off. From this the Sages said that if wicked people attack, one should bow his head and he will be saved. Gamliel said this showed how great the Sages' words are, that a wife may remarry if her husband fell into water with a visible edge but not with no edge.

terms.meaning: Jewish law.

yevamot-121a-19-19.note: Rabbi Akiva saw a boat sink and grieved for the Torah scholar aboard, Rabbi Meir. When Akiva landed in Cappadocia, Meir came and discussed law with him. Meir said one wave carried him to the next until one threw him onto dry land. Akiva said this showed how great the Sages' words are, that a wife may remarry if her husband fell into water with a visible edge but not with no edge.

terms.meaning: Jewish law.

yevamot-121a-7-7.note: Rabbi Yosei reports two incidents. A blind man went down into a cave to immerse for purity, his guide followed, and both vanished for long enough that they could not have survived, so the Sages let their wives remarry. In Asya, a man lowered into the sea on a rope came up as only a leg: if cut at or above the knee his wife may remarry, if below the knee she may not.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: the sage who reports the incidents

terms.meaning: To dip in a pool of water to become ritually clean.

yevamot-121b-5-6.note: The daughter of Nehunya the well digger fell into a large cistern, and people asked Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa to pray for her. After one, two and then three hours he told them she was fine, and then that she had come up. She said a ram and an old man leading it pulled her out. Asked if he was a prophet, he said no, and explained that he reasoned God would not let the righteous Nehunya's own child be harmed by his public service.

people.name: Nehunya the well digger
people.about: a righteous man who dug wells for the public

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: a sage known for his prayers

yevamot-121b-15-16.note: A gentile went around announcing that Hasa had drowned, and Rav Nahman said the fish had eaten him. Although Rav Nahman gave no formal ruling, Hasa's wife remarried and no one objected. Rav Ashi learned that the ban on remarrying after a drowning in endless water applies only at the outset; if she has already remarried, she is not taken from her husband. A second version says Rav Nahman did rule, reasoning that a great man would have been heard from; the Gemara rejects that reason.

terms.meaning: From the outset; before the act is done, as opposed to after the fact.

yevamot-121b-17-17.note: A gentile threatened a Jew that he would kill him like another Jew he said he had already killed. The dead man's wife heard this and asked Abaye if she could remarry, but he could not decide the case over three festivals. Rav Adda bar Ahava sent her to Rav Yosef, who compared it to a baraita saying a gentile's claims about fruit being forbidden carry no weight since he may only be boosting his sale. He concluded the gentile's statement here could not be relied on.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: described as having a sharp mind for legal matters

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

yevamot-122a-2-2.note: Abba Yudan of Sidon tells of a Jew and a gentile who traveled together. Later the gentile said, alas for the Jew who was with me, he died and I buried him. The Sages relied on this statement and allowed the man's wife to remarry.

people.name: Abba Yudan of Sidon
people.about: the one who reports the incident

yevamot-122a-3-3.note: Two more incidents are told. Prisoners in collars were walking to Antokhya, and later a gentile said they had died and he had buried them. Sixty people were walking toward the siege of Beitar, and later a gentile said the same. In both cases the Sages allowed the wives to remarry.

yevamot-122a-4-4.note: The Mishnah rules that a woman may be allowed to remarry on the word of a voice announcing her husband's death, even without seeing who spoke. In one incident, a person on a mountaintop announced that a named man had died. People went up and found no one there, yet they relied on the statement and allowed the man's wife to remarry.

terms.meaning: The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses.

yevamot-122a-5-5.note: In Tzalmon in the Galilee, a man called out his name and said a snake had bitten him and he was dying. People went and found his body but could not recognize it. They allowed his wife to remarry based on what he had said in his last moments.

yevamot-122a-10-12.note: Rabbi Akiva went to Neharde'a in Babylonia and met Nehemya of Beit D'li. Nehemya said he had a tradition from Rabban Gamliel the Elder that a court may let a woman remarry on one witness. Rabban Gamliel of Yavne welcomed this, saying the lenient view of Yehuda ben Bava now had support. He recalled the murdered men at Tel Arza and let their wives remarry on one witness. From then on hearsay, a slave, a woman and a maidservant were accepted, though Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva disagreed on some points.

people.name: Nehemya of Beit D'li
people.about: a sage Akiva met in Babylonia

people.name: Rabban Gamliel of Yavne
people.about: grandson of Rabban Gamliel the Elder

people.name: Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: the one sage who allowed one witness

terms.meaning: To add an extra month to the Jewish calendar so it stays in line with the seasons.

yevamot-122a-15-16.note: The Mishnah recounts that Levites traveling to Tzoar left a sick companion at an inn. When they returned, the woman innkeeper said he had died and she had buried him, and she brought his staff, bag and Torah scroll as proof. Based on her word his wife was allowed to remarry. Rabbi Akiva answered that a woman can be believed when she is as convincing as the innkeeper was. The Gemara explains she was a gentile who spoke offhandedly, and that her crying before being asked counted as the start of her account.

terms.meaning: Speaking casually, not meaning to testify, which makes a statement more believable here.
The later discussion of the Mishnah.

yevamot-122b-2-5.note: A man came to Rabbi Tarfon to testify that a woman's husband had died. He said they had traveled together, the husband drove off pursuing soldiers using a tree branch, and he called him lion. The dead man said that was indeed his name: Yohanan, son of Yonatan, the lion from Shihayya. He later fell sick and died. Rabbi Tarfon questioned the witness two or three times, found his answers consistent, and allowed the wife to remarry.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: the sage who heard the testimony

people.name: Yohanan, son of Yonatan
people.about: the man said to have died, called the lion

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.
